title: Initial ridge-spur lake-road practical travel scale
scope: Broad conditional fair-weather journey anchors for the established road between Project Hearthway's initial ridge-spur settlement and the lake; exact distance, journey distribution, road engineering, transport, traffic, shore infrastructure, seasonal impairment, institutions, encounters, and System effects remain open.
approval_evidence: On 2026-08-15 the Author replied, 'I choose B — Half-day working route for the practical lake-road travel scale.'
question: What broad practical travel scale should govern the already-established road between the initial ridge-spur settlement and the lake without fixing exact distance, route engineering, transport, seasonal performance, or guaranteed journey time?
selection: Use B — Half-day working route. Under the displayed fair-weather comparison, an ordinary unladen downhill journey has a broad 1–1½-hour reference band and a routine laden uphill return has a broad 2–3-hour reference band. A useful shore visit followed by a loaded return can consume most of a working day, while the lake remains part of regular settlement life. The bands are author-facing planning anchors, not exact, measured, minimum, maximum, scheduled, universal, or guaranteed journey times.
alternatives: A — Close daily orbit: 30–60 minutes downhill unladen and 1–1½ hours uphill laden; not selected.
B — Half-day working route: 1–1½ hours downhill unladen and 2–3 hours uphill laden; selected.
C — Outer daily reach: 2–3 hours downhill unladen and 4–6 hours uphill laden; not selected.
rationale: The selected scale best preserves the Author's fairly-far-but-not-too-far direction. It makes same-day lake activity credible while allowing burden, remaining daylight, shore work, delay, and environmental transition to matter, without requiring any particular vehicle, pack animal, road engineering, shore facility, institution, or encounter.
evidence: Author selection on 2026-08-15: 'I choose B — Half-day working route for the practical lake-road travel scale.'
consequences: The established lake road uses the author-facing practical scale half-day working route.
Under the displayed fair-weather comparison, an ordinary unladen downhill journey uses a broad 1–1½-hour reference band.
Under the same comparison, a routine laden uphill return uses a broad 2–3-hour reference band.
The direction and load qualifiers are inseparable from their respective bands; unladen ascent and laden descent remain undefined.
A useful shore visit followed by a loaded return can consume most of a working day while the lake remains part of regular settlement life.
The bands are author-facing planning anchors rather than exact, measured, minimum, maximum, scheduled, universal, or guaranteed journey times.

Actual journeys may fall outside the bands because of traveller condition, load, balance, terrain, rests, route knowledge, road condition, weather, season, daylight, obstruction, injury, or animal movement.

Exact distance, elevation change, gradient, road alignment, width, surface, drainage, engineering, maintenance, condition, seasonal impairment, route capacity, and journey-time distribution remain undefined.

No benchmark traveller, standard load, load weight, party size, vehicle, pack animal, traffic frequency, transport custom, gate endpoint, shore endpoint, landing, harbour, cache, shelter, outpost, or lakeshore settlement is established.
No fishing, gathering, fresh product, preservation method, trade, convoy, patrol, lodging, road authority, toll, ownership, customary schedule, or economic importance is established.

WLD-ECOLOGY-004 through WLD-ECOLOGY-006 remain contextual authorities; no exact habitat sequence, species presence, secondary-path overlap, predator encounter, obstruction, closure, injury, delay, loss, or journey outcome is established.
